families.s: HSE pipeline construction, inspection, maintenance and emergency-planning guidance
families.t: weld inspection, pressure testing, internal inspection, corrosion, good repair, emergency procedures, local authority plans, public warning and vulnerable groups
f: Pipeline welds should be inspected using suitable non-destructive examination before commissioning.
Testing should confirm construction quality and pressure integrity before operation.
Operators must maintain pipelines in good repair.
Internal inspection tools can identify deterioration and should be used at risk-based intervals where applicable.
Inspection results should drive corrosion assessment, repair and future inspection planning.
Pipeline operators must prepare and test emergency procedures for major accidents.
Local authorities prepare emergency plans for applicable major-accident pipelines.
Warnings and communication should consider affected communities and vulnerable groups.
families.g: Pipeline integrity and emergency risk depends on design and weld quality, testing, pressure and product, corrosion and damage, inspection capability, repair, emergency procedures, local plans and public warning.

families.s: HSE Mines Regulations operator and major-hazard control guidance
families.t: mine operator, goal-setting duties, major hazards, management structure, competence, rescue provision, general regulations and notifications
f: The Mines Regulations 2014 apply primarily to mine operators and focus on major-hazard control.
The mine operator is the principal dutyholder under the current regime.
General health and safety regulations continue to apply where they adequately cover the hazard.
Operators should establish suitable management structures, competence and control systems.
Mine-specific risks include fire, explosion, ground movement, inrush, shafts, winding, ventilation and escape.
All mine operators must maintain suitable rescue provision.
Specified events, commencement, abandonment and structural changes require notification to HSE.
The operator should retain evidence that major hazards are identified, controlled, monitored and reviewed.
families.g: Mine-operator risk control depends on mine type and layout, major hazards, management and competence, ventilation and ground control, rescue, notifications, monitoring and review.

families.s: HSE mine escape, emergency-plan, safe-haven and rescue guidance
families.t: escape routes, emergency plan, safe havens, communications, breathing conditions, rescue provision, training, exercises and mine-specific design
f: Mine escape arrangements should be based on the mine's specific layout, hazards and operating conditions.
The operator should prepare an emergency plan for foreseeable underground emergencies.
There is no single escape procedure suitable for every mine.
Routes, travel time, communications, breathing conditions and alternative exits should be assessed.
Safe havens may form part of the escape strategy where suitably designed and integrated.
Rescue arrangements should identify trained people, equipment, access and command.
Workers should be trained in alarms, escape, self-rescue and emergency responsibilities.
Exercises and reviews should test assumptions and update the plan after change.
families.g: Escape and rescue effectiveness depends on mine layout and depth, incident scenarios, route condition, ventilation and atmosphere, communications, safe havens, equipment, trained teams, exercises and review.

families.s: HSE mine shaft, winding, wire-rope and manriding guidance
families.t: vertical shafts, winding systems, wire ropes, safety switches, conveyances, manriding, inspection, maintenance and competent control
f: Mine shaft winding and manriding systems are safety-critical.
Wire ropes should be selected, installed, maintained and used for the actual shaft and duty.
Safety-related electrical switches in winding systems should meet suitable performance standards.
Conveyances, attachments, guides, brakes and controls require systematic inspection and maintenance.
Operating limits should reflect load, speed, rope condition and shaft geometry.
Manriding arrangements should control boarding, communication, movement and emergency recovery.
Defects affecting safe operation require the system to be stopped or restricted until resolved.
Competent people should oversee examination, testing, operation, maintenance and record keeping.
families.g: Shaft and winding risk depends on shaft and conveyance design, ropes and attachments, brakes and controls, load and speed, inspection and maintenance, safety switches, competence and emergency recovery.

families.s: HSE mine diesel-exhaust, dust and occupational-health guidance
families.t: diesel emissions, respirable dust, ventilation, enclosure, equipment maintenance, exposure monitoring, health surveillance, temperature and worker protection
f: Underground mining can expose workers to diesel-engine exhaust and respirable mineral dust.
Exposure controls should combine ventilation, source reduction and equipment maintenance.
Low-emission engines, suitable fuels and exhaust after-treatment can reduce diesel exposure.
Dust generation should be controlled at cutting, transfer, haulage and cleaning points.
Exposure monitoring should represent the worker, task and operating conditions.
Health surveillance may be required where residual respiratory risk remains.
Temperature and ventilation conditions can affect both health and safe work performance.
Records, worker information and investigation of abnormal results support continuing control.
families.g: Mine occupational-health risk depends on diesel and dust sources, ventilation, equipment condition, work pattern, exposure duration, monitoring, health surveillance, temperature and worker susceptibility.
